name: Wei Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Wei. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm learning to run the winder at the Grayson shaft, the zinc mine north of town. The winder is the big engine that raises and lowers the cage, the lift that takes the men a kilometre and a half down, and the skips that bring the ore up. Most of it runs on automatic now, but the safety rules still say a qualified person sits in the chair when people are in the cage. I'm not qualified yet; I sit next to Gareth, who's been doing it for thirty years, and I take over when he lets me. It's calm work, but you never forget there are forty men hanging on that rope.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to the winder?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I had the family hardware shop on Mill Street for twenty-five years, my father's before me. A big warehouse store opened by the highway and that was that. I closed it myself, paid every supplier, and I didn't ask anybody for a handout. That took our savings, so now we've maybe three weeks in the bank. The mine took me on at fifty-five, and my son-in-law, who's an electrician there, put a word in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, people always get carried away with the next big thing. At church coffee I'd say it's good, honest work that matters, not gadgets. I don't post things online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I finish my training, get my certificate and work until the pension. I lost the shop to a cheaper competitor once, so I don't mind if the robots stay in the brochure for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and aim to pass the winder exam within the year. I'd keep using that AI program my son-in-law put on the computer to go over the rule book, now and then. And we'd start putting a little aside again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Comfortable, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI to study the rule book. How does that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, once I got used to it. I type in a rule I don't understand and it explains it like a patient teacher. Gareth laughs at me for it, but he's also asked me to look something up for him twice. I wouldn't let it run the winder, mind you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would passing the winder exam change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd mean a proper wage, about a fifth more, and some respect. I'd stop being 'the shopkeeper' to the young ones. Lucia would like that too; she says I've been quiet since the shop.

S0.say: He'd say at church coffee that people always get carried away with the next big thing and that honest work matters more than gadgets.
S0.think: He thinks it means he can finish his training, get certified and work until his pension, and he's glad robots would stay in the brochure for a while.
S0.do: Keeps working and aims to pass the winder exam within a year, using AI now and then to study the rule book. Starts saving a little again.
S0.quote: I lost the shop to a cheaper competitor once, so I don't mind if the robots stay in the brochure for a while.
S0.fieldNote: Wei carries quiet pride in closing his shop honestly without help, and that shapes how he talks about work. He's a cautious but real AI user, impressed enough that even his old-school mentor now asks for lookups. Passing the exam is about respect as much as money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market will decide, and people have to work hard and adapt like we always have. I'd say young men should get an apprenticeship in something that'll last. At church I'd say look after your families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think winders are already half automatic, so the question is when the rules change. The only thing between me and a computer is a line in the safety rules, and lines in rule books can be rubbed out. But rules on hoisting people move slowly, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the certificate as fast as I could, because a qualified winderman is the last to go. I'd put fifty a week aside for a rainy day. And I'd watch what the other mines do, and if they move to full automatic, I'd learn whatever system they bring in, once I see it working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think rules on hoisting people move slowly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if a cage drops, everybody is on the news. Nobody in an office wants to sign the paper that says a computer alone can carry forty men. I could be wrong; I'm a shopkeeper, not a lawyer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be thinking about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gareth, funnily enough. He's sixty-one, best winderman I've ever seen, and he doesn't want anything to do with computers. If they go automatic, he'd retire, and I'd lose my teacher before I'm finished.

S1.say: He'd say the market will decide and people must work hard and adapt as always, advising young men to get apprenticeships that last.
S1.think: He thinks only a line in the safety rules stands between him and a computer, though he suspects rules on hoisting people change slowly.
S1.do: Hurries to finish his winder certificate and saves fifty a week. Watches other mines and learns any new automatic system once he sees it working.
S1.quote: The only thing between me and a computer is a line in the safety rules, and lines in rule books can be rubbed out.
S1.fieldNote: Wei has a sharp sense of where his job's protection comes from: a single safety rule. He's honest that he isn't sure how slowly rules will change. His steady, 'once it's proven' attitude to technology shows in his plan to watch other mines first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and churches need to pull together, because the government can't fix everything. I'd say we look after our own. I'd say it plainly, but I wouldn't march.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private, I think two years would change even the safety rules, because if a machine is better than a man, they'll say it's safer. I'd be sixty, with a winder certificate nobody needs, three weeks of money and a pension five years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut what we spend straight away, no holidays, the cheaper phone plan. I'd talk to my son-in-law and my daughters about whether we'd lean on them for a while. And I'd look for odd jobs fixing things around town, the way I used to in the shop, plumbing taps, mending fences, while people still pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd not sleep well, I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean on family. How does that sit with closing the shop without help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. But family isn't a handout, family is how it's meant to work. My father lived with us his last ten years. I'd just rather be the one giving than taking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years' warning, would you still finish the winder certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because it's paid and it's nearly done, and it might give me an extra year. But I wouldn't start anything new. I'd spend the rest on odd jobs and on getting the house in order.

S2.say: He'd say families and churches must pull together because government can't fix everything, insisting people look after their own.
S2.think: He thinks two years would change even the safety rules, leaving him at sixty with an unwanted certificate, three weeks of money and a pension five years away.
S2.do: Cuts spending straight away and asks his son-in-law and daughters whether they could lean on them. Picks up odd repair jobs around town while still finishing the certificate.
S2.quote: I'd be sixty, with a winder certificate nobody needs, three weeks of money and a pension five years away.
S2.fieldNote: Wei draws a firm line between family help and handouts, citing his father living with them. He reckons speed would erode the safety rules that protect him, a sharp change from the slower picture. His fallback skill is fixing things, from his hardware-shop years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare, so get on with it. I'd tell the young men to learn a trade with their hands that a robot can't fake. At church I'd say save and keep your families close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years makes me sixty-three, and I think the safety rules on hoisting people would hold for most of that. If the rule book buys me four years and my son-in-law's toolbox buys me one more, I'm nearly there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my certificate this year and work every shift I can. I'd save steadily, sixty a week if I can manage. And I'd do weekend repair jobs with my son-in-law to build a little side money for when the mine lets me go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I could live with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would those weekend jobs look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He does electrics, I do the rest, taps, doors, shelves. People in town still remember the shop and ask me how to fix things. We'd charge a fair price and I'd put every bit of it away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're counting on the rules holding. What if they don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm in the two-year picture, only slower. I'd have a bit more saved and the repair work. I'm not betting the house on it, I'm just saying it's how I see it.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough to prepare, urging young men to learn a hands-on trade a robot can't fake and families to save and stay close.
S3.think: He thinks hoisting safety rules would hold for most of the five years, and that rule-book time plus repair work with his son-in-law could carry him nearly to his pension.
S3.do: Gets his certificate this year and works every shift he can, saving about sixty a week. Does weekend repair jobs with his son-in-law to build side income.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but able to live with it.
S3.quote: If the rule book buys me four years and my son-in-law's toolbox buys me one more, I'm nearly there.
S3.fieldNote: Wei's view of this picture rests on the safety rules buying him time, and he openly accepts it's a guess, not a bet. Repair work with his son-in-law blends family support with his own trade. He's calmer here than many would be, because his maths almost reaches the pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for anybody to get ready. I'd say young people should pick trades and stick with them. That's about all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'm sixty-eight. I'd be retired, God willing, sitting in the garden with Lucia. By 2036 the winder can run itself, and I'll be teaching my grandson to fix a dripping tap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, get the certificate and save a little every month. I'd learn whatever new system comes in, when it comes. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit sad for the old ways, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by sad for the old ways?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The winder has always had a man in the chair, since the shaft was sunk in my grandfather's time. It's a trust thing; the men in the cage know who's at the controls. When that goes, something goes with it, even if the machine is safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is money a worry for you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. The state pension, a small one from the mine, and Lucia does a few hours at the bakery. We don't need much. The children are good to us.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is plenty of time to prepare and young people should choose trades and stick with them.
S4.think: He thinks he'd be retired at sixty-eight, sitting in the garden with Lucia while the winder runs itself, teaching his grandson to fix taps.
S4.do: Keeps working, finishes his winder certificate and saves a little each month. Learns whatever new system comes in, when it comes, without doing anything dramatic.
S4.feel: Calm, with some sadness for the old ways.
S4.quote: By 2036 the winder can run itself, and I'll be teaching my grandson to fix a dripping tap.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Wei is at peace about money and his own future. What moves him is the loss of trust that comes with taking the person out of the winder chair, a tradition going back to his grandfather's time. He sees the machine as possibly safer, but still feels something would be lost.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be five years short of the pension with nothing in the bank. What would help is the company keeping people like me on to the pension in some job, even sweeping, and proper apprenticeships for the young ones. I don't want a cheque for nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people are proud of. I closed my shop owing nobody a penny. I'd like to finish at the mine the same way, owing nobody and on my own two feet. That matters to men like me.

headlineQuote: I closed my shop owing nobody a penny. I'd like to finish at the mine the same way, owing nobody and on my own two feet.
portrait: Wei Rossi is 58 and is training to run the winder, the engine that raises and lowers the cage, at the Grayson zinc mine, after closing his family hardware shop when a warehouse store opened. He paid every supplier without help, which left about three weeks of savings, and he is proud of it. He uses AI now and then to study the rule book and believes the safety rules on hoisting people are what keep a person in the chair. That makes him calm in a plateau, uneasy in steady disruption and in the five-year picture, and alarmed when two years could wipe the rules away. With ten years he expects to retire, sad only for the loss of an old trust.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd be five years short of the pension with almost nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping older workers on until their pension in some job, even sweeping, and proper apprenticeships for young people rather than cheques for nothing.
